abstract: <jats:p>The importance of blue carbon is significant in terms of climate change mitigation and marine ecosystem conservation, and halophyte acts as a crucial reservoir for this blue carbon. Accordingly, this study utilized unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) optical sensors to create a distribution map of vegetation in the natural salt marsh of the Jujin estuary. The optical images captured from a UAV at an altitude of 50 m provide ultra-high-resolution optical information with a ground sampling distance of 0.6 cm. Based on these images, a U-Net model was trained to classify <i>Phragmites communis</i> and <i>Suaeda maritima</i>, generating a classification map of the mixed habitats of salt marsh plants. The areas of <i>Phragmites communis</i> and <i>Suaeda maritima</i> in the Jujin- Cheon region were found to be 6,653.23 m<sup>2</sup> and 1,409.08 m<sup>2</sup>, respectively. The classification results were validated using field control point data, confirming an approximate classification accuracy of 92%.</jats:p>
title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Photogrammetry Based Dataset of Halophyte Distribution in Jujin Estuary

abstract: <jats:p>Calcium plays a significant role in intracellular signaling. Calcineurin B-like proteins (CBLs) and their target proteins, CBL-interacting protein kinases (CIPKs) have emerged a calcium network responsing to stresses in plants. In this study, we cloned a CIPK gene, <jats:italic>SpCIPK8</jats:italic>, from the halophyte plant <jats:italic>Sesuvium portulacastrumand</jats:italic> L. Bioinformation analysis showed that the cDNA of <jats:italic>SpC</jats:italic><jats:italic>IPK8 </jats:italic>was 1344 bp and encoded 447 amino acids with a molecular weight of 50.72 KD and an isoelectric point of 7.19. One transmembrane domain exists in this hydrophilic protein. Phylogenetic analysis showed that SpCIPK8 was similar with AtCIPK8 in <jats:italic>Arabidopsis</jats:italic>.The expression level of <jats:italic>SpCIPK8</jats:italic> in stems was three times higher than that in roots and the level in leaves was two times higher than that in roots.</jats:p>
title: Isolation and Expression Analysis of a Putative CIPK Gene in Halophyte <i>Sesuvium portulacastrumand</i> L.

abstract: <jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>Two sympatric subspecies of the xerohalophyte <jats:italic>Atriplex canescens</jats:italic> Pursh. (Nutt.) were compared for 84 d in outdoor salinity trials in their native coastal desert environment in Sonora, Mexico. Subspecies <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> grows naturally on sea water in the high intertidal zone of estuaries while subspecies <jats:italic>canescens</jats:italic> grows on dunes. In lysimeter pot experiments, ssp. <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> exhibited 50% growth reduction when the mean root zone salinity reached 1160 mol m<jats:sup>−3</jats:sup> NaCl compared to just 760 mol m<jats:sup>−3</jats:sup> for ssp. <jats:italic>canescens.</jats:italic> When irrigated with sea water in a flood plot, ssp. <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> had 50% higher growth rates than ssp. <jats:italic>canescens.</jats:italic> The specialization of ssp. <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> for a saline environment was associated with greater net transport of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> from root to shoot, greater Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> accumulation in the leaves and a higher Na:K ratio in the leaves compared to ssp. <jats:italic>canescens.</jats:italic> On the other hand, the two subspecies achieved approximately the same degree of osmotic adjustment in the leaves, equal to two to three times the external salinity, and had similar water use efficiencies. Even at relatively low salinities, both subspecies accumulated larger quantities of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> for osmotic adjustment than K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>. The results suggest that breeding for Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> accumulation rather than exclusion might be the more effective strategy for improving salt tolerance of conventional crop plants.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Little is known about how upper marsh plants (growing in freshwater) will respond physiologically to sudden increases in salinity. In this study, we used experimental microcosms to evaluate changes in plant-water relations in the halophyte <jats:italic>Spartina patens</jats:italic> following increases in soil salinity (salinity levels: 15, 30, and 45). There was a delay (by 3–5 weeks) in the lowering of leaf water potential (ψ<jats:sub>leaf</jats:sub>), stomatal conductance (g), and tissue water content (θ) in plants subjected to salinities of 30–45. These physiological delays in plant-water adjustments following sudden increases in salinity may be an adaptation of <jats:italic>S. patens</jats:italic> that allows it to effectively exploit higher habitat elevations that receive intermittent seawater inundations without promoting costly physiological modifications.</jats:p>
title: Delayed modifications in plant-water relations in the coastal marsh halophyte Spartina patens following sudden increases in soil salinity

abstract: <jats:p>Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) are considered as bio-ameliorators that confer better salt resistance to host plants while improving soil biological activity. Despite their importance, data about the likely synergisms between PGPR and halophytes in their native environments are scarce. The objective of this study was to assess the effect of PGPR (<jats:italic>Glutamicibacter</jats:italic>sp. and<jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic>sp.) inoculation on biomass, nutrient uptake, and antioxidant enzymes of<jats:italic>Suaeda fruticosa</jats:italic>, an obligate halophyte native in salt marshes and arid areas in Tunisia. Besides, the activity of rhizospheric soil enzyme activities upon plant inoculation was determined. Plants were grown in pots filled with soil and irrigated with 600 mM NaCl for 1 month. Inoculation (either with<jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic>sp. or<jats:italic>Glutamicibacter</jats:italic>sp.) resulted in significantly higher shoot dry weight and less accumulation of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>and Cl<jats:sup>–</jats:sup>in shoots of salt-treated plants.<jats:italic>Glutamicibacter</jats:italic>sp. inoculation significantly reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) concentration, while increasing the activity of antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase; catalase; ascorbate peroxidase; and glutathione reductase) by up to 100%. This provides strong arguments in favor of a boosting effect of this strain on<jats:italic>S. fruticosa</jats:italic>challenged with high salinity.<jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic>sp. inoculation increased shoot K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>and Ca<jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>content and lowered shoot MDA concentration. Regarding the soil biological activity,<jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic>sp. significantly enhanced the activities of three rhizospheric soil enzymes (urease, ß-glucosidase, and dehydrogenase) as compared to their respective non-inoculated saline treatment. Hence,<jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic>sp. could have a great potential to be used as bio-inoculants in order to improve plant growth and soil nutrient uptake under salt stress. Indole-3-acetic acid concentration in the soil increased in both bacterial treatments under saline conditions, especially with<jats:italic>Glutamicibacter</jats:italic>sp. (up to +214%). As a whole,<jats:italic>Glutamicibacter</jats:italic>sp. and<jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic>sp. strains are promising candidates as part of biological solutions aiming at the phytoremediation and reclamation of saline-degraded areas.</jats:p>
title: Plant Growth-Promoting Rhizobacteria Alleviate High Salinity Impact on the Halophyte Suaeda fruticosa by Modulating Antioxidant Defense and Soil Biological Activity

abstract: <jats:p>The C<jats:sub>3</jats:sub> halophyte <jats:italic>Suaeda salsa</jats:italic> L. grown under the high concentration of NaCl (200 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic>) was used to investigate the role of the hydrogen peroxide (H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>)‐scavenging system [catalase, ascorbate peroxidase, glutathione reductase (GR), ascorbic acid, and glutathione (GSH)] in removal of reactive oxygen species. The activity of catalase (CAT, EC 1.11.1.6), ascorbate peroxidase (APX, EC 1.11.1.11), and GR (EC 1.6.4.2) increased significantly after 7 days of NaCl treatment. The isoform patterns of CAT and GR were not affected, but the staining intensities were significantly increased by NaCl treatment. Activities of both the thylakoid‐bound APX or GR and stromal APX (S‐APX) or GR in the chloroplasts were markedly enhanced under high salinity. Fifty percent of APX in the chloroplasts is thylakoid‐bound APX. S‐APX and GR activity represented about 74–78 and 64–71% of the total soluble leaf APX and GR activity, respectively. Salt treatment increased the contents of ascorbic acid and GSH. By contrast, a decreased content of H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> was found in the leaves of NaCl‐treated <jats:italic>S</jats:italic>. <jats:italic>salsa</jats:italic>. The level of membrane lipid peroxidation decreased slightly after NaCl treatment. The plants grew well with high rate of net photosynthesis under high salinity. These data suggest that upregulation of the H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>‐scavenging system in plant cells, especially in the chloroplasts, is at least one component of the tolerance adaptations of halophytes to high salinity.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Considering Korea’s gradual shift toward an aging society, consumer interest in compounds with physiological benefits, including antioxidant and anticancer effects, has surged. This study explored the potential of Tetragonia tetragonoides (Pall.) Kunze, commonly known as New Zealand Spinach (NZS), a halophyte with reported health benefits, including efficacy in treating gastrointestinal diseases, high blood pressure, diabetes, and obesity. This study also introduced a novel callus culture system for NZS, allowing for the rapid in vitro production of secondary metabolites. Optimal callus induction (100%) and biomass production (0.416 g) were achieved by adding 2.0 mg·L−1 6-BA (6-Benzylaminopurine) and 0.5 mg·L−1 2,4-D (2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) among five auxin and cytokinin combinations. Two distinct callus types, TGC [TDZ (Thidiazuron)-supplemented Green Callus] and TNYC [TDZ + NAA (Naphthalene acetic acid)-supplemented Yellow Callus], were identified, each with unique characteristics. The calli showed total phenolic and flavonoid contents comparable to those of NZS leaves grown in the greenhouse. An expression analysis of six genes (CHS, CHI, F3H, F3′H, FLS, and DFR) involved in the kaempferol biosynthesis revealed an enhanced flavonoid biosynthesis-related gene expression in TGC, emphasizing its potential for compound production. GC-MS analysis identified distinct compound profiles in TGC and TNYC, with 2,3-butanediol and succinic acid being the predominant compounds among the nine and forty-four components, respectively. These calli offer a stable supply of functional compounds and present an environmentally sustainable solution. The derived callus culture system is anticipated to contribute to the development of healthy functional foods or pharmaceuticals from halophyte NZS.</jats:p>
title: Exploring the Production of Secondary Metabolites from a Halophyte Tetragonia tetragonoides through Callus Culture
